For my 21st birthday, I've decided on getting a 1911, but I'm still unclear on the differences between series 70 and 80. My preference is more of a G.I. model.
I'm not sure exactly myself but IIRC it has to do with extractor type and how the saftey works.

In the early 1980s Colt introduced improved safety features that positively prevented the firing pin from moving forward unless the trigger was actually pulled (mainly to prevent accidental discharge in case the gun was dropped at just the right angle) and they referred to the newer guns as series 80. Virtually all 1911s built today incorporate the series 80 safety features. Series 70 referred to the spring fingered barrel bushing equipped Gold Cups and Commanders introduced in the early 1970s. It was supposed to make the mass produced guns more consistent out of the box, like match pistols with custom mated barrels and bushings.

If you're looking at new manufactured 1911s, they are almost guaranteed to have the series 80 improvements; and manufacturing improvements since the 70's have most gun makers producing guns with tight enough tolerances between the barrel and bushing, so you probably won't see many with the spring fingered bushing.

If you're looking at used guns, good luck. There are tons of frankenguns out there that range from amazing to dangerous, and if you aren't knowledgeable about the details of the gun and all the variants, or have a decent gunsmith to go shopping with you you're just spinning the roulette wheel.

Like you, I wanted my first 1911 to be a GI pattern gun. My first purchase was a Rock Island model that was a pretty close copy of the classic GI pattern.

I liked the gun - Rock Island has a good rep, and they deliver good value for the money - but there were two things about the pattern that I really did not like. The hammer bit the web of my hand, and the sights were tiny and almost useless. Worse, the small, rounded front sight was machined into the frame, and not easily replaceable.

I sold it and replaced it with a lightly-used Springfield GI Mil-spec, like this:

http://www.springfield-armory.com/products/1911-mil-spec-45-acp/

Despite the name, there are three significant difference from the GI pattern - real, usable sights, a slightly shortened hammer spur that does not bite, and a larger ejection port. It's exactly what I wanted and I love it.

Note that Springfield offered some similarly-named guns which were closer to the original pattern, so be careful not to get them mixed up if you choose to go that route.

I have also read on various forums that Colt 1911s are currently well-made and good values as well. They are not much more expensive than the Springfields, but I have no personal expense with them.

I think the fundamental problem is that these sites basically come down to content filters. The goal is to take hundreds to thousands of articles and then choose some fraction of a fraction of all of those to display. So of course the question is how are these select articles chosen? There's going to be problems any way you do it, but I think this system is particularly flawed. Most folks here do not navigate /v/all/new. It's generally full of turds and even when you do find an interesting article it's going to be new and so you won't find much discussion going on and in all probability there never will be any as it'll end up getting buried. So what happens is that the largest minority that does peruse the /v/new filters ends up choosing what content gets displayed for everybody.

When this is a random sample of the overall population this would be an awesome system, but it's not. I don't think most people here are your anti-black anti-immigrant anti-science anarchist far right extremists anymore than most people on Reddit are your authoritarian anti-free-speech anti-white anti-straight far left extremists. Yet on both sites both groups control a share of the message space that is far disproportionate to their actual numbers, since they disproportionately make up the folks dragging new content up. A simple solution would be to start having a few wild-card slots on the front page where new content is randomly placed. Basically give buried content a chance to rise to the top without having to have people wade through the /v/new filters. A far more technically challenging, but potentially far more effective, solution is automating the scoring system. There are a ton of metrics you can use and weight in various ways. In fact it's a perfect scenario for a deep learning AI. Drop our bickering by bringing on the robot overlords. It'd also be something entirely revolutionary among social media boards if it actually ended up working effectively. And of course there are many other ideas, but just relying on a nonrandom active minority to be a representative sample of the userbase as a whole clearly just doesn't work.
